name: Port Hedland
title: Port Hedland Hull Gauging: UTM for Capesize Ore Carriers
description: Thickness gauging at Port Hedland for capesize ore carriers, salt, spodumene and livestock ships: holds, hopper and ballast tanks, decks and hatch coamings.
h1: Thickness Measurement for Bulk Carriers at Port Hedland
intro: Port Hedland is Australia's largest bulk export port by tonnage, and almost everything it ships is iron ore, loaded into capesize bulk carriers at the BHP, Fortescue and Roy Hill berths for steel mills in North Asia. These ships shuttle between the Pilbara and China, so a loading call is often the only time an owner can collect readings between dockings. There is no repair yard in the region; our technicians travel from India through Perth for each job and gauge the ship at its berth or while it waits offshore.

highlights.h: Readings sized to the tide and loader
highlights.p: Ore loads quickly at Port Hedland and departures are fixed to the tide, so the gauging scope is built around the berth window and any waiting time at anchor. Priorities are agreed in advance, and the team works through the most important spaces first.

highlights.h: Holds that carry the heaviest cargo
highlights.p: Iron ore is dense and often carried in alternate holds, so the inner bottom, hopper plating and lower frames of the loaded holds take the most punishment. Grab damage at the discharge ports adds mechanical wear to corrosion, and both show up in thickness readings.

highlights.h: Cyclone season can close the port
highlights.p: Between November and April a tropical cyclone can close Port Hedland at short notice, with ships ordered off the berths and out to sea. A job booked in that season carries a weather plan, and the team holds back until the port reopens.

port.h: Port Hedland: a tidal harbour built around iron ore
p: Port Hedland is a natural tidal harbour on the Pilbara coast, reached from the Indian Ocean through a long dredged channel. The tidal range is large, and the depth a loaded capesize needs is only available around high water, so departures run to a tight sequence with sailing drafts set by under-keel clearance calculations. Ships arriving in ballast usually wait at the anchorage offshore until their berth and tide line up, then come in with pilots and tugs. Once loaded, they leave on the next suitable tide, often one after another in a planned procession. This rhythm shapes everything about working on a ship here: time alongside is short and predictable, time at anchor can be longer but depends on the queue, and the sea state offshore decides whether a launch can reach a waiting ship at all.

The private iron ore berths dominate. BHP loads at Nelson Point and Finucane Island, Fortescue at Anderson Point through its infrastructure subsidiary, and Roy Hill at Stanley Point, where the berths are limited to ships below a set maximum length. Alongside them, the public berths managed by Pilbara Ports serve a more varied trade. Berth PH3 has a shiploader used for Dampier Salt's exports, berths PH1 to PH3 also handle livestock, general and heavy-lift cargo and petroleum products, and berth PH2 is designated for ammonium nitrate bound for the mines. The Utah Bulk Handling Facility at berth PH4 is a multi-user bulk berth for manganese, iron ore from smaller producers and spodumene, the lithium-bearing concentrate that has become a significant Pilbara export. That mix brings Supramax and Panamax bulk carriers, livestock carriers and small tankers into a port otherwise defined by capesizes.

Most capesizes calling here are owned by Asian and European shipowners and chartered by the miners or by trading houses, and charterers screen them through vetting systems such as RightShip before fixing. A ship that shows corrosion problems at a Pilbara berth, whether found by the crew, a vetting inspector or a port state control officer, can lose business quickly. The voyage pattern adds its own stress: short laden passages, quick loading and grab discharge in Chinese ports mean ballast tanks cycle constantly and holds are worked hard. Owners therefore use Port Hedland calls for intermediate checks on the spaces most likely to deteriorate, and for pre-docking estimates on ships heading to a Chinese yard. Buyers of second-hand capesizes sometimes arrange pre-purchase gauging here too, since the ship's position and schedule are fixed and predictable.

facilities.h: Ore berths, public berths and the offshore anchorage
p: There is no dry dock, slipway or repair yard for deep-sea ships at Port Hedland, or anywhere else on the Pilbara coast. Capesizes on the China trade normally dock in Chinese yards, so the work done here is preparation and monitoring rather than docking-period gauging. At the ore berths, the miners control access to their terminals, and each has its own induction, permit and protective equipment rules. The team therefore has to be registered with the right terminal before the ship arrives, and the agent confirms the berth well ahead. On deck, gauging works around the shiploader: hatch coamings, deck plating and cross-deck structure on holds not under the loader, and ballast tanks once deballasting has emptied them and the atmosphere has been tested.

The anchorage offers more time but less certainty. A ship waiting for its berth is in ballast with empty holds, which is ideal for hold and hopper gauging, but launch transfers in open water depend on the swell and the wind, and the run out to the ship takes time. The public berths are the most flexible part of the port: salt carriers, livestock carriers and general cargo ships may stay longer than a capesize, which allows a wider scope. Whatever the berth, the job is planned around the tide table, because the ship will sail when the water is there whether or not the gauging is finished.
list: BHP berths at Nelson Point and Finucane Island: deck, coaming and ballast tank gauging on capesizes within the loading window
Fortescue's Anderson Point and Roy Hill's Stanley Point berths: priority readings on holds not yet under the loader
Utah Bulk Handling Facility (PH4): hold and hopper gauging on bulk carriers before spodumene, manganese or ore loading starts
Public berths PH1 to PH3: wider scopes on salt carriers, livestock carriers and general cargo ships during longer stays
Offshore anchorage: hold, hopper and topside tank gauging by launch on ships waiting in ballast

context.h: AMSA, ballast water and the Pilbara cyclone season
p: AMSA carries out port state control at Port Hedland as at every Australian port, under the Tokyo MoU and the Indian Ocean MoU. With so many bulk carriers loading in the Pilbara, AMSA inspectors see a great deal of the world's capesize fleet here, and the condition of cargo holds, hatch covers and their securing arrangements, air pipes and access ladders comes under regular scrutiny. Loading itself is governed by the BLU Code and the ship's loading manual, and a ship with wasted hopper plating or cracked frames in its ore holds is carrying risk into every laden passage. Thickness readings that show how close the inner bottom and hopper structure are to their renewal limits give owners a basis for deciding whether a repair can wait for the next docking.

Two other regimes affect ships arriving here. The Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry requires international arrivals to report their biofouling management through the Maritime Arrivals Reporting System, and it enforces Australia's ballast water requirements, which matter a great deal at an export port where ships arrive in ballast and discharge it while loading. Constant ballasting is exactly what breaks down tank coatings, so ballast tank gauging is the core of most jobs. The second regime is the weather: the Pilbara Ports cyclone procedure sets out how the port clears ships from the berths and the anchorage when a cyclone approaches, and the port has closed for cyclones in recent seasons. A job booked for the wet season is planned with room to move.

jobs.h: Typical gauging jobs at Port Hedland
jobs.p: Port Hedland jobs are short, focused and planned closely. The most common is an intermediate check on a capesize's ballast tanks, hopper tanks and ore holds, fitted into one loading call and continued at later calls if the scope is large. Pre-docking estimates for Chinese yard periods come next, followed by pre-purchase gauging for buyers of second-hand bulk carriers and condition surveys on the smaller ships at the public berths. We set the priorities with the superintendent, register the team with the terminal, follow the ship's ETA through the agent, and travel from India so the team reaches the town before the ship berths. Reports are issued on the class TM formats.
list: Ballast and hopper tank gauging on a capesize during one loading call, completed over two Port Hedland visits to cover the full scope
Pre-docking steel estimate on an ore carrier heading to a Chinese yard, concentrating on inner bottom, hopper plating and hold frames
Pre-purchase gauging of a capesize at the anchorage while it waits in ballast for its berth
Hold and hatch coaming gauging on a Supramax before it loads spodumene at the Utah Point berth
Condition gauging of decks and tanks on a livestock carrier loading cattle at a public berth

logistics: The team flies from India to Perth and on to Port Hedland International Airport on a domestic flight. An Australian visa suitable for short-term specialist work is arranged before departure, and its lead time is built into the plan. Accommodation in Port Hedland is often tight because of the resource industry, so it is booked as soon as the ETA is reasonably firm. The agent arranges port passes, and each miner's terminal sets its own induction; visiting technicians work under the terminal's escort or visitor arrangements.

faqs.q: Is a Port Hedland loading call long enough for useful gauging?
faqs.a: For a focused scope, yes. A capesize may be alongside for less time than at many other ports, so we agree a priority list with the superintendent: usually the ballast tanks that are already empty, deck plating and coamings, and holds before they receive cargo. A larger programme can be split across successive calls, because ships on the Pilbara to China shuttle come back regularly.

faqs.q: Can ballast tanks be entered while the ship is deballasting?
faqs.a: Only once a tank is empty, ventilated and tested, and entered under the ship's enclosed-space entry permit. The order in which tanks empty is set by the loading and deballasting plan, so we follow it rather than ask the ship to change it. Tanks that empty early can be gauged during loading; those that empty last may have to wait for the anchorage or the next call.

faqs.q: What happens if a cyclone threatens Port Hedland during a booking?
faqs.a: The port's cyclone procedure takes over: ships are moved off the berths and the anchorage, and port activity stops until the authority reopens it. If a cyclone is forecast before the team travels, we hold the mobilisation; if one arrives during the job, the team stands down safely ashore and resumes when the ship returns. Wet-season bookings are always planned with that possibility in mind.

faqs.q: Where do Port Hedland ore carriers go for dry docking?
faqs.a: Most capesizes trading to China dock in Chinese yards, and some in Southeast Asia. Nothing on the Pilbara coast can take them. That is why readings taken at a Port Hedland call are so useful before a docking: they give the owner a steel estimate to put in the yard specification, and a basis for questioning the yard's own figures once the ship is in dock.
